transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-30
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Kim (Redwood AE), Devon Patel (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Aurora - Head ML Infra), Elena Torres (Aurora - Platform Eng), Rahul Gupta (Aurora - CTO)

Summary: Technical deep dive focused on running megacontext workloads (>128k tokens) in Aurora's on-prem VPC. Covered chunking strategies, attention sharding, KV caching / eviction policies, batching trade-offs, quantization profiles, and enterprise networking/security constraints for private deployments. Action items and next steps agreed.

Topics: megacontext chunking, attention sharding, KV cache & eviction, continuous batching, quantization options (Q4, int8), on-prem/VPC deployment, KMS/HSM integration, perf benchmarking plan

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Sofia Kim: Hey everyone thanks for taking the time, um we know you wanted a deep, like really deep, dive into long context performance — so Devon and I will jump in. Marcus, Rahul, Elena, you there?
[00:08] Marcus Lee: Yep here, thanks Sofia. We're pretty excited, this is kind of make-or-break for a couple products, so appreciate it.
[00:13] Rahul Gupta: Morning/afternoon all. Quick context: Aurora is planning a customer-facing assistant that must ingest multi-document manuals up to ~150k tokens and keep full fidelity answers with retrieval + appended context.
[00:24] Elena Torres: And network wise we'll be in our colo VPC with strict egress rules, we can't just go to public hosted endpoints.
[00:30] Devon Patel: Perfect — that's the scenario we designed our private package around. Quick raise: are you aiming to pin a single model family or want dynamic model routing (size/quant variants)?
[00:40] Marcus Lee: We started with a 16B family for cost reasons, but if quant + sharding gives us better economics the team is open. Primary ask is consistent p95 latency under 3s for interactive flows, batch jobs can be looser.

[00:55] Devon Patel: Great. So at a high level for mega context (>128k) we generally recommend a hybrid chunking approach: do application-level semantic chunking to split docs into coherent windows, then use lightweight in-memory append + KV cache for active prefixes. That way you keep the "hot" state in cache and avoid reattending the entire history.
[01:15] Marcus Lee: When you say KV cache, you mean the per-request key-value cache that stores past keys/values in GPU memory? Any differences between your hosted runtime vs private?
[01:24] Devon Patel: Yes. Our KV cache is GPU-resident by default — we support multiple layouts: monolithic cache for single-GPU runs, and sharded KV across GPUs for runtime sharding. On private, we also offer a persistent prefix store option backed by local NVMe which speeds cold-starts. Note that persistent store is on-disk and has higher latency than GPU-resident cache.
[01:45] Elena Torres: How do you handle eviction? Our workloads have a very long tail, hotspots shift, and we don't want cache thrashing.
[01:52] Devon Patel: Good question. We use a two-tier policy: LRU-ish for sequence segments and MRU weighting for very recent tokens — plus we expose cache window sizing and prefetch hints. For megacontext, we recommend prefix pinning for doc heads you know will be referenced a lot. Also support for sparse retention where tokens marked as "summary" are stored compressed.
[02:12] Rahul Gupta: Sparse retention — is that lossy? Will it impact beam-scored answers?
[02:17] Devon Patel: It's lossy for raw-token reconstruction but we keep semantic embeddings so retrieval remains high quality. For exact quoting you would keep the raw tokens pinned. Tradeoff is memory.

[02:30] [timestamp jump - short audio glitch]
[02:36] Marcus Lee: I'm concerned about attention compute — full attention on 150k is astronomic. What real options do we have?
[02:42] Sofia Kim: Put another way: you shouldn't run quadratic dense attention across all 150k tokens. You edge toward a mixture: local windowed attention, long-range sparse attention (segment-level), and attention interpolation like cosformer / linearized blocks. Devon?
[02:56] Devon Patel: Yeah — we typically use block-sparse attention plus hierarchical pooling. Practically we implement a two-stage mechanism: first do chunk-level compressive attention to produce chunk summaries (small vectors), then attend with a lightweight cross-attention to the summaries for global context. That reduces compute and KV size dramatically.
[03:16] Elena Torres: How do you map that to GPU kernels, any custom kernels or is it standard aten ops?
[03:21] Devon Patel: For our runtime we have specialized kernels for block-sparse matmuls and fused qkv attention when sequence lengths exceed 32k. We also have a kernel path that streams attention in tiles to avoid OOM and use async DMA to keep the pipeline fed. On public cloud GPUs we leverage vendor primitives; in private we provide a compile step that tunes kernels to the exact hardware.
[03:44] Marcus Lee: That compile step — does it require a full model recompile? How long does it take?
[03:49] Devon Patel: It's model-to-runtime optimization — typically 15–45 minutes for a new model binary and hardware target; incremental re-tuning is faster. It picks kernel tiling, memory layout, and whether to enable fused attention.

[04:05] Rahul Gupta: On quantization — we've seen Q4_K_M and some int8 variants. Which do you recommend for keeping semantics with megacontext? We're worried about hallucination growth.
[04:15] Devon Patel: Our recommendations: use mixed precision — Q4_K_M for keys/values to reduce KV footprint and int8 or float16 for activations depending on your hardware. For long-context, preserving precision in the attention softmax and position encodings is important, so keep those in higher precision. Also run small evals: we provide an eval harness that compares log-prob deltas and end-task metrics.
[04:38] Elena Torres: Do you have any empirical numbers on token throughput differences between Q4_K_M and int8 on, say, an Llama-like 16B at 64k?
[04:45] Devon Patel: Rough ballpark: Q4_K_M can reduce KV memory by ~50% and give a modest 1.2–1.5x throughput improvement when KV bandwidth is the bottleneck. Int8 activation quant can give 1.6–2.2x for compute-bound paths. But exact numbers depend on sequence distribution and whether you're IO or compute bound.

[05:10] Marcus Lee: Okay. Now, routing and batching: we need interactive p95<3s but also want to batch for cost. How do you balance continuous batching without violating SLOs?
[05:20] Devon Patel: We use latency-aware batching: small, latency-first windows for interactive traffic — batching for tokens within a single request and opportunistic merging of very short requests. For high-throughput backfills we use large batch windows. There's also a hybrid mode where we keep a single-slot interactive lane that preemptively pulls in GPU resources and a batch lane for CPU tolerant loads.
[05:40] Elena Torres: Is preemption handled at kernel-level? What happens to partially completed requests?
[05:45] Devon Patel: We preempt at scheduling boundaries; long-running batches are checkpointed and can be resumed — we never kill user-facing interactive requests. Preemption adds some overhead but maintains SLOs.

[05:58] Rahul Gupta: On networking — for private VPC installs we require all egress blocked and KMS in our control. How does Redwood integrate with customer KMS/HSM?
[06:07] Sofia Kim: We have pluggable KMS hooks. For Private installs we can integrate with AWS KMS, Google KMS, HashiCorp Vault, or on-prem HSMs. Keys never leave the HSM; the control plane talks to an operator-managed KMS endpoint. We also support local key wrapping for air-gapped setups.
[06:21] Marcus Lee: And audit logs? Our compliance folks want immutable, tamper-evident logs for per-request data access.
[06:27] Sofia Kim: Our private control plane ships with a hardened audit subsystem, write-once logs to your S3 or object store, and can forward signed events to your SIEM. We also have per-token usage breakdowns in the Console for economists.

[06:40] [07:00] Marcus Lee: Could you show a sample perf run configuration? Like, what exact flags do you flip for a 150k workload?
[07:05] Devon Patel: Sure I'll paste a short one in the shared doc after, but high-level: enable block-sparse attention, set block size to 1024 for chunking, enable KV-sharding across 4 GPUs, use Q4_K_M on KV, keep activations fp16, set batch low-latency threshold to 12ms, and enable prefix pinning for the first 4k tokens of each doc.
[07:24] Elena Torres: When you say KV-sharding across 4 GPUs — does that mean model parallelism or just cache sharding?
[07:30] Devon Patel: It's cache sharding, separate from model sharding. You can run model replica per GPU and shard the KV across them, which avoids cross-device allgather for KV lookups. It reduces network hops but requires co-located GPUs with RDMA or NVLink ideally.

[07:45] Rahul Gupta: If our colos don't have NVLink between the four A100s, will RDMA over RoCE be fine?
[07:51] Devon Patel: RDMA RoCE is acceptable; it introduces slightly higher latency than NVLink but still within tolerances for many workloads. We recommend 100Gbps fabrics and careful tuning of MTU and NIC offloads.

[08:05] Marcus Lee: About persistent prefix store — if we persist the KV to NVMe, how does cold start look? If a user brings a document that's rarely accessed, what's latency?
[08:14] Devon Patel: Cold start from NVMe to GPU is proportional to the data size; typical range for a 10k-token prefix moved from NVMe into GPU is 20–80ms depending on NVMe bandwidth and PCIe gen. For 100k+ it's more costly — which is why we recommend semantic summaries for cold tails and only pull full raw tokens when needed.

[08:34] Elena Torres: Any suggestions for chunking strategy? We've tried fixed 4k chunks which end up splitting paragraphs awkwardly.
[08:40] Devon Patel: Yes — avoid pure fixed chunks for prose. We recommend a hybrid: sentence-boundary aware tokenization to keep paragraphs intact, then a sliding overlap of 128–512 tokens between chunks to preserve cross-boundary attention. For code or log files, fixed chunks are OK. Also consider semantic anchors: identify section headings and pin them as chunk boundaries.

[09:05] [09:15] Marcus Lee: Are there tooling recommendations for chunking? Off-the-shelf libraries?
[09:18] Sofia Kim: We have a small open-source toolkit we can share that does sentence-aware chunking + overlap and produces anchor metadata for retrieval. We'll add it to the shared folder.

[09:28] Rahul Gupta: Let's talk scale. If we put this behind a customer-facing assistant, we might have 20 QPS peak. With your recommended config, how many GPUs per QPS?
[09:38] Devon Patel: Very workload-dependent, but for interactive 16B with our optimizations and 150k context, you're looking at a few hundred ms per token when hitting summaries mostly. For an approximate back-of-envelope: one 80GB A100 might sustain ~6–10 interactive QPS with latencies in your target if requests are mostly summary-lookups. If every request forces full 150k token reconstruction, throughput drops to <1 QPS.

[10:05] Elena Torres: So the real engineering effort is making sure the majority of requests hit the cache/summaries, not the full dense history.
[10:11] Marcus Lee: Right, we need clear cache hit metrics and alerting.

[10:18] Devon Patel: Console supports token-level cache hit metrics, per-route throttles, and can emit alerts on p95 regressions tied to a prompt set. We'll also provide a set of evaluation prompts that measure summary-fidelity and hallucination rates.

[10:32] [10:40] (crosstalk)
[10:42] Marcus Lee: What's the easiest way to simulate our production distribution? We have very spiky tails.
[10:48] Sofia Kim: Send us your real prompt traces redacted — we'll run perf sims in our lab and give a capacity plan. That's part of the pilot.

[10:55] Rahul Gupta: On security again — is data-movement encrypted in memory between GPUs? We're in a regulated vertical.
[11:01] Devon Patel: Intra-node memory traffic depends on fabric; NVLink is point-to-point and not encrypted by default. We support memory encryption on certain hardware via vendor features and can enable TLS+mutual auth for inter-node RDMA. For high compliance we recommend isolation per-tenant and dedicated hardware.

[11:20] Elena Torres: Could you expand on per-tenant isolation? We're thinking multiple teams will use this cluster.
[11:25] Devon Patel: You can run Dedicated pools: separate GPU pools per tenant, or use a multitenant pool with strict RBAC and ephemeral sandboxing of model weights and KV. Dedicated pools are simplest for compliance.

[11:38] Marcus Lee: Let's talk failure modes. If a GPU goes down mid-session, how do you resume?
[11:44] Devon Patel: We checkpoint KV state periodically and replicate critical prefixes across GPUs. If a GPU fails, requests route to a fallback replica with a slightly cold cache; latency spikes while the fallback warms up. For strict SLAs we recommend active-active replicas with sync'd prefix metadata.

[11:59] Sofia Kim: Quick check — does this all match the regulatory constraints you mentioned earlier?
[12:05] Marcus Lee: Yes, mostly. We need to confirm the HSM integrations and the audit log immutability. We'll need a write-up for our security reviews.

[12:13] Devon Patel: We'll include a SOC2/ISO-ready appendix and HSM integration docs in the shared folder.

[12:20] [12:30] (short silence as notes are taken)
[12:34] Elena Torres: A couple of nitty-gritty: how do you estimate memory for KV if you do chunk-level summaries? We want a predictable estimator to plan capacity.
[12:42] Devon Patel: Our estimator: KV_mem ≈ N_chunks * chunk_summary_size + live_token_kv * per_token_kv_size. For summary size we use 256–1024 floats depending on compression. We'll provide a spreadsheet and a small CLI calc that takes your avg chunk size, summary embedding dims, retention window and outputs memory + expected bandwidth.

[13:02] Marcus Lee: Great. Also curious about model rollouts. Can we A/B older dense-attention model vs new sparse one?

[13:08] Devon Patel: Yes — Redwood supports route-level rollouts, canarying, and automatic fallback. You can route a small percentage of traffic to the new sparse path and automatically compare outputs with the baseline, including diff metrics for hallucinations and log-prob deltas.

[13:25] Rahul Gupta: Any gotchas for logging and privacy? If we log token-level data, how do you redact PII?
[13:32] Sofia Kim: We provide configurable redaction hooks and can run on-host redaction before sending events to the control plane. There's also a mode where only aggregated token telemetry is sent.

[13:42] [13:50] (noise, small laugh)
[13:52] Marcus Lee: Can we see a demo of the streaming with a megacontext prompt?
[13:57] Devon Patel: We can demo a reduced-size example now — full 150k would take a while. I'll show a 60k flow that uses chunk summaries and live KV.

[14:08] [DEMO START]
[14:10] Devon Patel: (screen) Sending a prompt that contains multiple docs, first watch the KV hit markers on the console — you can see the prefix hits and the summary fallbacks.
[14:20] Marcus Lee: I see the console showing hits and cold pulls. There's a spike at 14:23 — what triggered that?
[14:26] Devon Patel: That was a cold fetch of a pinned heading we hadn't loaded. You can see the measured time to pull from NVMe to GPU.
[14:32] Elena Torres: Nice. And the streaming tokens start at 14:37 — latency looks good.
[14:37] Devon Patel: This is smaller scale, but it demonstrates the same scheduling and preemption logic you'd use in private.
[14:45] [DEMO END]
[14:50] Marcus Lee: That helps. On the cost side, any guidance for cost modeling? We need a clear way to show finance.
[14:57] Sofia Kim: We'll include a cost model: per-GPU run-rate, expected amortized per-token cost given hit-rate assumptions, and a sensitivity table for hit-rate vs. QPS. We also have a whitepaper for batch vs interactive lanes.

[15:10] Rahul Gupta: A couple quick questions from engineering: 1) Do you support dynamic sequence-length kernels that avoid re-padding? 2) Can we get a detailed timeline for the private deployment pilot?
[15:21] Devon Patel: 1) Yes we optimize for dynamic sequence lengths and avoid unnecessary padding where the kernel supports it. 2) For private pilot: week 0 we run a discovery (config + capacity planning), week 1–2 deploy control plane + test infra, week 3 pilot runs and perf sweeps, week 4 handoff. We'll adjust depending on your procurement.

[15:40] Elena Torres: Procurement is always the slow bit — legal wants SAML, IP retention clause, and data deletion SLA.
[15:47] Sofia Kim: We have templates that cover SAML SSO, retention SLAs, and clear clauses for data. We'll share those with your legal and procurement team.

[15:56] [16:00] Marcus Lee: If we move forward, what does success look like in 30 days?
[16:03] Devon Patel: For the pilot success criteria: a) you can run representative prompts on private infra with p95 within target (or documented tradeoffs), b) cache hit-rate above agreed % for typical flows, c) integration with KMS and audit logs verified, and d) agreed rollout plan.

[16:20] Rahul Gupta: Sounds good. Couple more specifics: can you run a perf sim with our mix and show tail latencies and GPU occupancy?
[16:26] Sofia Kim: Yes, that's part of the lab run — we'll accept a redacted trace and return a capacity plan and a perf-run artifact.

[16:34] [16:40] (discussion about scheduling next meeting)
[16:44] Marcus Lee: Let's aim for pilot kickoff week of Oct 12. We'll share the prompt set by Oct 4.
[16:50] Sofia Kim: Perfect. We'll follow up with the runbook and the sample configs. Devon will also include the demo notes.

[16:56] [Wrap-up]
[16:58] Elena Torres: Thanks, this was super helpful and very concrete.
[17:01] Marcus Lee: Appreciate it.
[17:03] Rahul Gupta: Thanks everyone.
[17:05] Sofia Kim: Great — we'll send follow-ups and the doc pack.
